standard.title: Analysing Contested Historical Interpretations
standard.description: analyse different and contested historical interpretations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse different and contested historical interpretations in a Year 9 inquiry context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse different and contested historical interpretations, construct arguments about which interpretation is best supported by evidence, and evaluate how interpretations change over time.

nodes.label: Identifying and evaluating competing interpretations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different historical interpretations of the same event or period and construct an argument about which interpretation is better supported by the available evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different interpretations of the same event or period and construct an argument — with evidence — about which is better supported.
nodes.typical_width: Explore debates about the historical period or topic studied — such as the 'Brisbane Line', 'reds under the bed' and McCarthyism's influence in Australia; identify different interpretations and construct evidenced arguments for which is best supported; apply evaluative language in historical argument (to what extent, however, in contrast, the evidence suggests).
wider: Apply interpretation analysis to a topic where First Nations and non-Indigenous historians have produced competing accounts — such as the Frontier Wars or the significance of the 1967 Referendum — evaluating how the historian's standpoint and methodology shapes the interpretation produced

Examine how the same debate is framed by a professional academic historian, a public historian (museum curator, documentary maker) and a political commentator, evaluating how purpose and audience shape the interpretation offered
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can only identify competing interpretations without constructing an evidenced argument for one cannot complete the extended historical argument required by S08. The move from 'there are different views' to 'view X is better supported because...' is the prerequisite for independent historical argument.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly teach the structure of an interpretive argument: state the interpretation, provide supporting evidence, acknowledge the competing interpretation, explain why the evidence favours one over the other. Model this with a specific historical debate from the course before expecting independent construction.

Apply interpretation analysis to debates involving First Nations historians alongside non-Indigenous historians — this is the most analytically rich application context in the Year 10 course, directly connecting S07 skills to the K-strand civil rights content.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Contested interpretation analysis applied to First Nations historiography is one of the most sophisticated and consequential analytical challenges in the course — it connects the abstract skill of interpretation analysis to the concrete, high-stakes debates of Australian history.
success_criteria: Identify at least two different historical interpretations of the same event or period
Construct an argument — using evidence — about which interpretation is better supported
Use evaluative language correctly in the argument (e.g. 'to what extent', 'however', 'the evidence suggests')

nodes.label: How interpretations change over time
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how historians have changed their interpretations over time and construct a historical argument that identifies different interpretive possibilities.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how at least one historical interpretation has changed over time, explaining what drove the change; construct a historical argument that acknowledges different interpretive possibilities while presenting a clear position.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how historians have changed the way they interpret an event under investigation over time — such as a change in view with the discovery of more sources, changes in methodology, or changes in the social context of historical writing; construct a historical argument that identifies different interpretive possibilities, organises ideas to build an argument, presents a particular point of view with consistent reference to available evidence, and uses evaluative language.
wider: Trace the full historiography of a contested topic across at least three decades — mapping how the dominant interpretation has shifted as new evidence, new methodologies, and changing social contexts have influenced historical writing

Compare how the 'history wars' debate in Australia (over colonial history and the Stolen Generations) developed and was resolved or remained contested, examining what the debate reveals about the relationship between historical interpretation and political context

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the interpretation identification (Node 1) with a more sophisticated understanding of how interpretations are produced and how they change — bringing together source analysis skills (S03–S04), perspective analysis (S06), and interpretation analysis (Node 1) into a full historiographical understanding.

success_criteria: Describe how a specific historical interpretation has changed over time and explain what drove the change
Construct a historical argument that identifies different interpretive possibilities while clearly presenting one position
Explain how new sources, new methodologies, or changing social contexts can change historical interpretation
